newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian police say $57 mln MinFins frozen in June.
newsitem.headline: Russian police say $57 mln MinFins frozen in June.

text.p: A Russian police officer working on a case involving frozen MinFin bonds said on Monday that his prosecutor's office had issued an order to freeze $56.81 million face value in June.

This would bring the total bonds currently known to have been frozen to $74 million, including around $24 million already detailed by the finance ministry in July. Some bonds are included in both lists of frozen securities.

Mikhail Ignatyev, a detective in the investigations department of the fifth central Moscow police precinct, told Reuters that the $57 million of bonds had been frozen in connection with an investigation into a small bank which has since been closed down.

Of these $6.93 million were already included on a list of $24.22 million of bonds frozen from March until May. This list was released by the Finance Ministry in July, so Ignatyev's list contains around $50 million worth of new bonds.
It was not clear whether some bonds were frozen twice at different times in connection with different orders, or simply appeared on two different lists.
Rumours that more than $24 million of the dollar-denominated bonds had been frozen started circulating last Monday, pushing down prices by nearly two big figures.
Liquidity in the market dried up as spreads widened, and trading is now mainly being conducted through brokers.
Officials from the Finance Ministry and Vneshtorgbank, the main MinFin depositary, have made no official comments on the latest trouble to hit MinFins.
Banks holding the MinFins have also refused to comment on whether they had been advised that their bonds had been frozen.
An official at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Moscow told Reuters that the bank had been advised by the depositary only last week that bonds on the June list had been frozen.

The initial freezing of $24 million of missing bonds, some of which had been stolen in the breakaway republic of Chechnya, hit prices hard by undermining investor confidence in the willingness of Russia's authorities to service its debt.
But MinFin prices had risen steadily in recent months in the run-up to the launch of Russia's debut Eurobond, planned for later this month.
The issue has still not been revised by the judicial authorities on the one hand and the Finance Ministry, central bank and Vneshtorgbank on the other.
